report.title: Example Usability Report — Library Self-Service Borrowing

metadata.method: Moderated usability observation and heuristic evaluation
metadata.goal: Observe how a first-time library user borrows three items, responds to a borrowing error, prints a receipt, and leaves the station ready for the next user. The session considers the touchscreen, scanner, physical layout, feedback, instructions, and surrounding service experience.

findings.location: Borrowing station > Start screen / card reader
findings.description: The participant paused at the start screen and looked between the touchscreen and the physical card reader before asking where to begin. The screen says 'Begin session', while the card reader separately says 'Present card', making the first action ambiguous.
findings.why: The station presents two possible starting points without clearly communicating which action should happen first. The participant's hesitation indicates that the intended sequence was not immediately understandable.
findings.recommendation: Use one clear first-step instruction that visually connects the screen and reader, such as 'Scan your student card to begin', and remove or subordinate competing start instructions.
findings.evidence: Participant paused for approximately 8 seconds, looked at both components twice, then asked: 'Do I press this first or scan my card?'

findings.description: The participant repeatedly moved a large art book around the scanning surface because the active scan zone is narrow and positioned close to the rear edge of the desk. The book obscured the on-screen instructions while being positioned.
findings.why: The physical target for successful scanning is comparatively small and awkward to reach with a large object. The size and placement of the interaction area increases physical effort and makes successful target acquisition less predictable.
findings.recommendation: Increase the effective scanning area or provide a clearly marked larger placement zone. Position the scanner so large books can be placed without covering the display or requiring precise alignment.
findings.evidence: The first book scanned immediately. The larger book required four repositioning attempts before registration.

findings.description: After an item is scanned, the station gives a quiet tone but the visual confirmation appears in a small list at the side of the screen. The participant scanned the same book twice because they did not notice that the first scan had succeeded.
findings.why: The system does not make the result of the scanning action sufficiently visible or noticeable at the moment it occurs. The user cannot confidently determine whether the system has registered the item.
findings.recommendation: Provide immediate prominent confirmation near the primary task area, combining a visible success state with an audible cue. Temporarily show the title and a clear 'Item added' message after each successful scan.
findings.evidence: One duplicate scan attempt occurred. Participant said: 'I don't know if it got that one.'

findings.description: When a reference-only item is scanned, the station displays 'Transaction unavailable — code 214'. The participant does not know whether the problem relates to their account, the scanner, or the book, and attempts to scan the item again.
findings.why: The message identifies neither the cause of the problem nor an appropriate recovery action. The internal error code is not meaningful to the library user.
findings.recommendation: Replace the code-led message with plain-language guidance: identify that the item cannot be borrowed, explain why where appropriate, and direct the user to the service desk or another available action.
findings.evidence: Participant rescanned the item twice and then looked toward the staffed desk for assistance.

findings.description: After scanning several books, the participant is unsure whether selecting 'Finish' will complete the borrowing process or merely finish adding items. There is no clear indication of the current stage or what will happen next.
findings.why: The station does not provide enough context about where the user is in the overall borrowing sequence or the consequence of moving forward.
findings.recommendation: Show a simple process state such as '1. Identify > 2. Scan items > 3. Review & finish', and rename the action to communicate its consequence, for example 'Review borrowing'.
findings.evidence: Participant hovered over Finish, withdrew their hand, reread the screen, then asked whether they would still be able to check the item list.

findings.description: The final screen preselects 'Print receipt'. The participant normally uses digital library records and does not want a paper receipt, but continues without noticing the selected option and produces an unnecessary printout.
findings.why: The default adds an avoidable physical output and assumes a preference that may not reflect common user behaviour. Because the choice is already selected, it is easy to overlook.
findings.recommendation: Use a neutral receipt choice with no preselection, or make the lower-impact digital/no-print option the default if supported by service data. Clearly show the selected state before completion.
findings.evidence: Participant noticed the receipt only after it printed and said: 'I didn't realise I'd chosen that.'

findings.location: Borrowing station > Receipt printer / collection point
findings.description: The receipt printer is mounted below the desk and slightly to the side of the touchscreen. After the screen reports that a receipt has printed, the participant searches around the station because the collection point is not visible from their standing position.
findings.why: The physical output location is part of the interaction but is not visually signposted. The user must discover the location by searching rather than through an obvious affordance or cue.
findings.recommendation: Add a visible label and directional cue near the screen, illuminate the receipt slot when printing, and consider relocating the output point into the user's normal field of view.
findings.evidence: Participant looked behind the monitor and at the adjacent station before noticing the receipt below the desk.

findings.description: After borrowing is completed, the account summary remains visible until the user presses a small 'End session' control. The participant assumes the process is finished and begins to walk away while their name and borrowed-item information remain on screen.
findings.why: The user is not given a sufficiently clear and safe exit from the authenticated state. The system's session remains active even though the user's task appears complete.
findings.recommendation: Make session completion explicit and prominent. Automatically sign out after the final confirmation where appropriate, or present a dominant 'Finish and sign out' action before the user leaves.
findings.evidence: Moderator stopped the session after the participant moved approximately two steps away from the kiosk with account information still displayed.

findings.location: Borrowing area > Queue and adjacent stations
findings.description: The stations are positioned closely together with screens angled toward the shared queue. During account identification and error recovery, the participant repeatedly glances toward nearby users and lowers their voice when asking for help.
findings.why: Although the borrowing task can be completed, the spatial arrangement reduces comfort and confidence by making personal account activity feel exposed to people waiting nearby.
findings.recommendation: Review station spacing, screen angles, privacy filters, and queue position. Create clearer personal-use zones so users can complete borrowing and resolve problems without feeling observed.
findings.evidence: Participant commented after the task: 'It feels like everyone behind me can see what I'm doing.'

findings.location: Borrowing station > Help and staff assistance
findings.description: The station provides a small '?' icon for help, but its content only explains touchscreen functions. When the participant encounters the restricted-item error, the help content does not explain library borrowing rules or how to obtain staff assistance.
findings.why: Help exists, but it does not support the actual problem encountered during the task. The user needs contextual guidance that connects the interface problem to the wider library service.
findings.recommendation: Provide context-sensitive help for common borrowing problems and include a clear route to human assistance, such as 'Ask library staff at the service desk' with directional information.
findings.evidence: Participant opened Help after the error, scanned the first help screen, closed it, and then approached the staffed desk.
